title: Pediatric TTP: Congenital Upshaw-Schulman Syndrome vs Immune ADAMTS13 Deficiency
subject: ss-paediatric-nephrology

steps.say: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is caused by severe functional deficiency of the von Willebrand factor cleaving protease.
steps.tx: Understand the central molecular defect driving **ADAMTS13 deficiency and vWF multimers** in thrombotic microangiopathy. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) results from a severe functional deficiency of ADAMTS13 (a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with thrombospondin type 1 motifs, member 13), defined as plasma activity < 10%; absent protease activity prevents normal cleavage of ultra-large von Willebrand factor (ULVWF) multimers, precipitating spontaneous microvascular platelet agglutination and widespread microthrombosis.

vis.alt: Ultra large von Willebrand multimers forming platelet microthrombi and schistocytes.
vis.caption: TTP: uncleaved multimers, microthrombi and schistocytes. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Severe congenital deficiency manifests in neonates and young infants as Upshaw-Schulman syndrome.
steps.tx: Recognize the genetic presentation of **Congenital TTP (Upshaw-Schulman syndrome)** during early pediatric life. Congenital TTP (Upshaw-Schulman syndrome, cTTP) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the ADAMTS13 gene on chromosome 9q34; it characteristically manifests in the neonatal period or infancy with severe Coombs-negative hemolytic jaundice, profound thrombocytopenia, and exchange transfusion dependency, often triggered by minor viral infections or childhood vaccinations.

right.title: Childhood Triggers
points: Precipitated by routine vaccines or febrile illness

steps.say: Acquired autoimmune TTP occurs in older children and adolescents mediated by neutralizing autoantibodies.
steps.tx: Evaluate autoantibody-mediated pathophysiology in **Acquired/immune TTP (iTTP) in adolescents** presenting acutely. Acquired immune TTP (iTTP) is mediated by IgG autoantibodies (inhibitors) directed against ADAMTS13, predominantly seen in adolescent females and frequently associated with systemic lupus erythematosus or other autoimmune diseases; presentation is marked by acute, explosive microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, severe consumptive thrombocytopenia, and fluctuating neurological deficits.

vis.alt: Autoantibodies against ADAMTS13 with multimer strings and red cell fragmentation.
vis.caption: Immune TTP: autoantibody blocks ADAMTS13. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: The classic pentad includes fever, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological signs, and renal injury.
steps.tx: Identify the multi-system manifestations of the **Classic pentad of TTP** during emergency evaluation. The complete pentad comprises microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA with abundant schistocytes on blood film), severe thrombocytopenia, fluctuating neurological symptoms (ranging from headache and confusion to focal seizures and coma), fever, and mild renal impairment; however, only the dyad of unexplained MAHA and thrombocytopenia is required to initiate emergent therapy.

steps.say: Immediate therapeutic plasma exchange with fresh frozen plasma is life-saving and drastically reduces mortality.
steps.tx: Institute emergency resuscitation using **Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) urgency** without delaying for confirmatory assays. Emergency therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE, 1.0-1.5 plasma volumes daily replaced with fresh frozen plasma or solvent-detergent plasma) is life-saving in acquired iTTP, removing anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibodies and high-molecular-weight vWF multimers while replenishing active ADAMTS13 protease, reducing acute mortality from > 90% down to < 10-15%.

nodes.label: Draw baseline ADAMTS13 activity and inhibitor
Initiate daily TPE (1-1.5 plasma vol) + steroids immediately

steps.say: Children with congenital deficiency require regular prophylactic plasma infusions every two to three weeks.
steps.tx: Prescribe maintenance therapy with **Plasma infusion prophylaxis in congenital TTP** for long-term health. Because patients with Upshaw-Schulman syndrome lack antibodies and merely require protease replacement, they do not require plasma exchange; lifelong prophylactic fresh frozen plasma infusions (10-15 mL/kg every 2-3 weeks) or recombinant ADAMTS13 (apadamtase alfa) successfully prevent recurrent ischemic episodes and progressive organ damage.

steps.say: Anti-vWF nanobodies rapidly block platelet-multimer interaction and halt microvascular thrombosis.
steps.tx: Incorporate targeted biologics including **Caplacizumab and rituximab in immune TTP** to achieve rapid remission. In pediatric patients with acquired iTTP, modern regimens combine daily plasma exchange and high-dose corticosteroids with rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody at 375 mg/m² weekly for 4 doses to eliminate inhibitor-producing B-cell clones) and caplacizumab (an anti-vWF A1-domain humanized bivalent nanobody that rapidly prevents ULVWF-platelet adhesion).

vis.title: Adjuvant Biologic Agents in Immune TTP
rows: Binds vWF A1 domain to block GP1b
Stops microthrombi within hours, prevents stroke

steps.say: Transfusing platelets in active TTP can fuel widespread fatal thrombosis and is strictly contraindicated.
steps.tx: Enforce strict clinical prohibition regarding **Platelet transfusion contraindication in TTP** during acute flares. Platelet transfusions are strictly contraindicated in active TTP because infusing exogenous platelets provides immediate substrate for circulating ultra-large vWF multimers, precipitating catastrophic widespread microthrombosis that can cause sudden acute myocardial infarction, fatal stroke, and rapid clinical deterioration (unless life-threatening hemorrhage is present).

left.title: Dangerous Practice
points: Prophylactic platelet transfusion for low count
Precipitates fatal stroke and myocardial infarction

right.title: Correct Management
points: Permit transfusion only for catastrophic bleeding
Prioritize immediate plasma exchange and immunosuppression
